core.title: Keep secret literals out of source
core.given: A source or template file that the secret scan covers
core.when: The file contains an AWS access key id, a PEM private-key header, or a password/api-key/token assigned a literal string, whether the literal is new or was already there
core.then: Source MUST NOT contain a secret literal.
prefer: Move the value to the environment and read it at the edge through the stack's environment access idiom
If the literal was ever committed, rotate the credential. Removing the line is not enough.
avoid: Writing a working credential inline, even temporarily to get unblocked
Treating deletion of a committed secret as the fix, because version control history keeps it
unless: The file is a placeholder/example file per the profile's placeholder patterns. These are documentation, not secrets.
The file is in a tree the stack never scans (vendored or generated trees on the stack's single exclusion list).
The value is read from the environment through the stack's environment access idiom. This is never a literal and is not matched.
core.why: Version control keeps a committed secret, so deleting it does not fix it. Only rotating it does, which is why detection has to happen before the commit rather than in review.
evidence: The stack's secret scan reports no credential-literal finding on any covered source or template file
Credentials in covered files are read from the environment through the stack's environment access idiom
For any secret that was previously committed, the credential has been rotated (not just deleted)
verification: Disposition strict, severity 4; no baseline policy is inferred — a finding is never tolerated, it must be fixed.

A content-level scan of covered source and template files (existing and newly written content alike; each realization's checker decides which concrete files count as source and template) for five credential-literal patterns: AWS access key ids, PEM private-key headers, and password / api-key / token assigned a string literal. It applies to any literal present in a covered file, not only newly added ones.

Matching reads assignment shape, not entropy: it catches the realistic case of a working credential pasted inline to get unblocked, and deliberately does not judge whether a random-looking string is secret.

Scope exclusions are owned by the stack's checker: skip placeholder files matching the profile's placeholder patterns; never scan the trees on the stack's single exclusion list (vendored and generated trees); do not match values read through the stack's environment access idiom.

The patterns are language-neutral — the credential formats and the assignment shape are identical across stacks — so every realization of this core produces the same findings. The detector, validator and finding identifiers remain realization details.

values: AWS access key id, PEM private-key header, or password/api-key/token assigned a string literal present in a covered file

fires: A covered source or template file assigns a string literal to a variable or field named password, api key or token
A covered source or template file contains an AWS access key id, whether or not it is assigned to anything
A covered source or template file contains a PEM private-key header, whether or not it is assigned to anything
A secret literal was already in a covered file before the current change
doesNotFire: The credential is read from the environment at the edge
The literal sits in a placeholder/example file per the profile's placeholder patterns
The file is in a tree the stack never scans (the stack's single exclusion list)

A random-looking string that matches none of the patterns: it is not an AWS access key id, not a PEM private-key header, and not assigned to a password/api-key/token name. Entropy alone is not judged.

neutralityNotes: AWS access key id and PEM private-key header are kept verbatim: they are credential formats, orthogonal to stack, and the rule's own audit confirms the five patterns port verbatim between stacks; weakening them to 'a cloud key' would change the detected set. 'git' is generalized to version control history (same obligation). The concrete environment access idiom, placeholder file patterns and never-scanned trees are profile data; two keys (suffix.placeholder, idiom.security#env_access) had to be proposed because the closed vocabulary has no fit. Coverage of source and template files stays in the neutral activation as stack-neutral file-kind labels: bun.json names the covered kinds but enumerates no suffixes or filename patterns, so suffix.source / suffix.markup are not claimed (each realization's own checker decides which concrete files count as source and template, and a realization that does enumerate suffixes may populate those keys itself). Detector, validator and finding identifiers (bun_security_hygiene_detector, SECURITY-HARDCODED-SECRET-001) remain realization details; core verification describes the check generically.
